newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak NBS says its moves to be corrected.
newsitem.headline: Slovak NBS says its moves to be corrected.

text.p: The Slovak central bank (NBS) on Wednesday said some of the moves it had taken against bank IRB a.s. should be "corrected" at the bank's upcoming extraordinary general shareholders' meeting.
Until January, the NBS had tried to reverse several moves taken by the bank and its main shareholders including ownership issues and board changes.

But NBS Governor Vladimir Masar said:"We have received an announcement about the IRB's extraordinary shareholders meeting which will take place...(which) should also correct certain measures, which the NBS had taken through its decisions against the IRB".
Masar did not elaborate, though he did say that talks between the NBS and IRB, which had been prompted after the controversial acquisition of a large stake in IRB by steel maker VSZ, were "ongoing".
In January, IRB said it had replaced its president and three other board members upon request by its majority owners, but it did not elaborate, prompting NBS requests for clarification of the moves.
Last October, the NBS said VSZ must reverse moves it had taken since mid-1996 to take control of IRB's supervisory board, ruling the takeover illegal.

VSZ officially holds 14.6 percent of the bank and controls one-third of the seats on its supervisory board, but often works in an alliance with many of the bank's other shareholders on major decisions.

Last August, VSZ asked for central bank permission to increase its stake in IRB to over 20 percent but the central bank rejected the request saying "VSZ did not present its own plan on participation in restructuring process in the bank."
IRB is included on a government list of strategic companies as well as being part of a group of banks that will undergo loan portfolio restructuring.

The state holds a 35 percent stake in IRB through its privatisation agency the National Property Fund (NPF). VSZ is a major client of IRB, accounting for an estimated 1.5 percent of the bank's total loan portfolio.

VSZ accounts for 16 percent of Slovakia's industrial output with its steel works alone and has some 100 subsidiaries, limited companies. It has said it needs to have close ties to banks to ensure the financing of its ambitous expansion plans.
